Athletics.current_status: Funding for athletic complex improvements is currently being considered separately from the main budget and will be addressed at a later date. This follows a proposal to install a synthetic surface to enhance usability and access for student-athletes.
Athletics.overview:
On April 30, 2025, it was clarified that funding for athletic complex improvements is not part of the upcoming June 10th budget vote and will be addressed separately at a later date. This decision follows a presentation on January 8, 2025, where Athletics Director Todd Livingston advocated for a synthetic surface at the stadium complex. He presented data indicating that 78% of student-athletes utilize the stadium and argued that a synthetic surface would significantly increase playable hours, reduce cancellations, and enable more teams, such as field hockey, to practice and compete on campus.

Earlier, on March 28, 2024, a Board member raised concerns regarding equity and accessibility within athletics, specifically questioning admission fees for events and policies requiring students to purchase essential gear, like swimsuits, which could create barriers to participation for some families. Prior to this, on March 25, 2024, the Athletics Director provided a comprehensive overview of the department, detailing 25 high school and 18 middle school programs, highlighting mid-40% high school participation rates, numerous coaching and student awards, and a new partnership with Huddle for live-streaming and game analysis.

The Board and Administration also recognized athletic achievements on June 10, 2024, with a special acknowledgment of the Boys Outdoor Track and Field team for winning the state championship.

perspectives.Board: A Board member expressed concerns on March 28, 2024, about equity and accessibility in athletics, specifically regarding admission fees and the requirement for students to purchase essential gear, which could create participation barriers. The Board also participated in recognizing athletic achievements, including the Boys Outdoor Track and Field team's state championship on June 10, 2024.
perspectives.Administration: On January 8, 2025, Athletics Director Todd Livingston presented data supporting a synthetic surface for the stadium complex, emphasizing increased playable hours and team access. On March 25, 2024, the Athletics Director provided an overview of the department's programs, participation rates, awards, and a new partnership. The Administration also honored the Boys Outdoor Track and Field team for their state championship on June 10, 2024.

Equity.current_status: The SPSD Board unanimously approved a new Educational Equity Policy on June 8, 2026, which includes a crucial data collection component to understand and address systemic issues. This policy formalizes the district's ongoing commitment to equity.
Equity.overview:
On June 8, 2026, the SPSD Board unanimously approved the new Educational Equity Policy, following strong support from a teacher on the district's equity committee who emphasized the policy's crucial data collection component for understanding and addressing systemic issues. This approval marks a significant step in formalizing the district's commitment to equity.

Prior to this, the district grappled with complex equity issues surrounding elementary school reconfiguration. On April 29, 2026, principals presented community feedback revealing a tension between prioritizing equity, particularly for communities like Kaler and Skillin, and maintaining neighborhood schools. The board deliberated delaying reconfiguration until the 2027-28 school year, weighing the need for more planning against the urgency to address equity and promises made to the Kaler community. This discussion built upon earlier debates on revisiting reconfiguration as a cost-saving measure (December 17, 2025) and addressing stark demographic disparities between schools like Skillin and Small (October 15, 2024), which prompted board members to express frustration over the slow pace of addressing long-known inequities (October 15, 2024). The board had previously discussed potential long-term solutions like grade-level reconfiguration and controlled choice to create more balanced learning environments (April 8, 2024), with recommendations for expert impact studies on these models presented on February 12, 2024.

The district's broader commitment to Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) has been a recurring theme. On May 30, 2024, Or Men Gildo Paolo was hired as Director of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion, following the resignation of the previous DEI Director, Mohammad Albi Hadley, due to a racist email incident (January 22, 2024). The Superintendent pledged to continue DEI work with urgency (January 22, 2024), and the Assistant Superintendent updated the board on the DEI action plan, including the formation of an internal equity team and staff affinity groups (March 11, 2024). Other equity initiatives include addressing accessibility barriers in athletics, such as admission fees and equipment costs (March 28, 2024), and reaffirming the district's commitment to safety for all students amidst concerns over ICE activity (January 12, 2026).

perspectives.Board: Board members unanimously approved the new Educational Equity Policy on June 8, 2026. They have expressed conflicting emotions regarding elementary school reconfiguration, weighing the urgency of addressing equity issues and promises to the Kaler community against the need for more planning time (April 29, 2026). Some members expressed frustration over the slow pace of addressing long-known inequities, while others advocated for a thoughtful, well-planned solution (October 15, 2024). Members have debated the tension between maintaining neighborhood schools and creating integrated learning environments, with some willing to disrupt the status quo for greater equity (April 8, 2024). Concerns were also raised about equity and accessibility in athletics (March 28, 2024).
perspectives.Administration: The Superintendent reaffirmed the district's commitment to safety for all students amidst concerns over ICE activity (January 12, 2026). Principals presented findings from community listening sessions on elementary school reconfiguration, highlighting the tension between equity and neighborhood schools (April 29, 2026). The Superintendent presented data revealing stark demographic disparities between elementary schools (October 15, 2024). The administration hired Or Men Gildo Paolo as Director of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (May 30, 2024) and the Superintendent publicly condemned a racist act that led to the resignation of the previous DEI Director, pledging to continue DEI work with urgency (January 22, 2024). The Assistant Superintendent updated the board on the DEI action plan, including forming an internal equity team and launching Halal certified meals (March 11, 2024). The administration committed to investigating and removing financial barriers in athletics (March 28, 2024).
perspectives.Staff: A teacher from the district's equity committee strongly supported the new Educational Equity Policy, emphasizing the crucial role of its data collection component (June 8, 2026). Staff, particularly from Kaler and Skillin, often prioritized equity in discussions about elementary school reconfiguration (April 29, 2026). The Administrators' Association read a statement in solidarity with Mohammad Abbi Hadley, renewing their commitment to DEI work (February 12, 2024).
perspectives.Citizens: Public comment on April 29, 2026, revealed a deeply divided community regarding elementary school reconfiguration, with some parents and teachers urging immediate action to address inequity and others advocating for delay due to concerns about neighborhood schools. Public calls were made for accelerated staff training and clearer public guidance to support vulnerable families amidst ICE activity (January 12, 2026). Citizens connected the departure of the DEI Director to broader equity issues, stressing that 'shuffling numbers is not enough' and emphasizing the critical need to recruit and retain diverse staff (February 12, 2024). A community leader was quoted arguing against solutions involving busing students from already fragile families (April 8, 2024).

FY2025 Budget.current_status: The district is currently facing a projected FY2025 budget deficit of $1.3 to $1.9 million, primarily due to the financial impact of newly ratified staff contracts. An immediate non-personnel spending freeze has been implemented to curtail discretionary spending.
FY2025 Budget.overview:
The district is currently grappling with a projected FY2025 budget deficit, estimated between $1.3 and $1.9 million, as reported by the Finance Committee on December 8, 2025. This deficit is primarily attributed to the financial impact of newly ratified teacher and staff contracts. In response, the district has implemented an immediate non-personnel spending freeze for the remainder of the school year to curb discretionary spending.

Prior to this, South Portland voters passed the school budget referendum with a significant 22% margin of support on June 18, 2025, following a community reminder from the Superintendent on May 12, 2025. The FY2025 budget process was complicated in March 2025 by a last-minute, higher-than-expected 7.5% health insurance rate increase, which added an unforeseen $200,000 deficit to the Superintendent's proposed budget, then approximately $73 million with a 5.98% operating increase.

Earlier in the process, on May 13, 2024, the board had unanimously approved a $69.28 million FY2025 school budget to proceed to a city-wide referendum. This approval followed revisions presented by the administration on April 8, 2024, which utilized savings from lower-than-expected health insurance costs, resulting in a 4.88% increase and proposed additions including a new district-level Mental Health and Student Intervention position, additional stipends, and funds for security upgrades. Initial budget proposals in March 2024 ranged from $69.4 million to $69.5 million, consistently featuring a 5% operating increase and a projected 3.8% to 3.82% school tax rate increase, with the Superintendent highlighting the difficulty due to the loss of COVID-era funds.

perspectives.Board: The board expressed a strong desire on March 24, 2025, to keep the final tax impact at or below a 6% increase. On May 13, 2024, the board systematically voted on and unanimously approved the initial $69.28 million FY2025 school budget for referendum.
perspectives.Administration: The Superintendent and administration consistently presented various budget proposals, ranging from $69.4 million to $73 million, emphasizing a 5% operating increase and a 3.8-3.82% school tax rate increase as fair to taxpayers and lower than neighboring districts (March 2024). They highlighted challenges such as the loss of COVID-era funds and rising fixed costs, including a significant health insurance rate increase (March 2024, March 2025). The administration presented revisions to the budget on April 8, 2024, to incorporate savings and propose new positions and security upgrades. The Superintendent reminded the community of the referendum on May 12, 2025, expressed gratitude for its passage on June 18, 2025, and implemented an immediate non-personnel spending freeze on December 8, 2025, in response to a projected deficit.
perspectives.Citizens: South Portland voters demonstrated strong support for the FY2025 school budget, passing the referendum with a significant 22% margin on June 18, 2025.

FY2026 Budget.current_status: The FY2026 budget is currently projected to land closer to a small surplus or deficit, an improvement from earlier fears due to a district-wide spending freeze, though the final outcome awaits an audit.
FY2026 Budget.overview:
The financial outlook for the FY2026 budget has improved significantly from earlier projections. On July 20, 2026, the Finance Director reported that a district-wide spending freeze has led to a projection of the budget landing closer to a small surplus or deficit, rather than the previously feared worst-case scenario, though the final audit is still pending. This follows a November 3, 2025, update where the Finance Director noted a projected $337,000 deficit for FY2026, which was expected to be offset by a one-time $815,000 geothermal tax credit. However, a warning was issued at that time regarding the district's nearing depletion of its fund balance, posing significant challenges for the subsequent FY2027 budget.

Prior to these updates, the FY2026 budget was formally approved. On June 3, 2025, a special meeting was held where the board approved 19 budget action items for the FY2026 school budget, totaling $73,131,556, a procedural step expedited to meet the City Council's schedule. The Superintendent had reminded the public about the June 10th school budget referendum for the 2025-2026 school year on April 30, 2025, encouraging community participation. The initial budget proposal, presented on April 7, 2025, and further detailed on March 31, 2025, included a 5.98% operating budget increase, framed as a necessary response to the district's lowest projected student enrollment in 15 years. This $73 million budget was projected to require an additional $3.18 million from taxpayers, with health insurance costs (budgeted at a 5% increase) identified as a significant variable.

The development of the FY2026 budget began with significant financial challenges. On March 17, 2025, and March 10, 2025, the Superintendent presented a proposed budget requesting a $3.17 million increase from taxpayers for a total school operating budget increase of just under 6% ($72.9M), despite significant proposed reductions. Key budget drivers contributing to a potential $9 million shortfall included the loss of COVID-era and other carryover funds, contractual salary increases for three bargaining units, and rising health insurance costs. As early as February 24, 2025, the Superintendent outlined a challenging budget context, noting that a simple rollover of current services would necessitate an 11.4% local increase, citing pressures from expiring federal funds, rising special education needs, and reduced philanthropic funding. At that time, a non-essential spending freeze was already in effect, and reductions in employee positions were anticipated.

perspectives.Administration: The Administration, through the Superintendent and Finance Director, consistently presented the budget proposals, highlighted the significant financial challenges including expiring federal funds, rising special education needs, contractual salary increases, and increasing health insurance costs. They communicated the necessity of a 5.98% operating budget increase despite proposed reductions, and later reported on the positive impact of a district-wide spending freeze. Warnings were also issued regarding the depletion of the district's fund balance and its implications for future budgets. A non-essential spending freeze was implemented early in the process, and anticipated staff reductions were noted.

FY2027 Budget.current_status: The SPSD Board has unanimously passed the FY2027 budget, which incorporates a 6% tax impact and addresses the district's financial stability, with the City Council forgiving up to $2 million of the current year's deficit. A resolution to delay the reconfiguration timeline was also approved.
FY2027 Budget.overview:
On April 29, 2026, the SPSD Board unanimously passed all articles of the FY2027 budget. The Finance Director detailed the budget, emphasizing the district's precarious financial state and the need for long-term stability, noting the City Council's offer to forgive up to $2 million of the current year's deficit and their guidance to maintain a 6% tax impact, which the board adopted. In a separate 5-1 vote, the board also approved a resolution to delay the reconfiguration timeline, establishing a steering committee and committing to a final vote on the implementation plan by November 2026.

This unanimous approval followed a previous rejection of the Superintendent's proposed FY2027 budget on March 30, 2026, which failed in a 2-5 vote. Board members voting against it expressed concerns over specific personnel cuts (including DEI, special education, and arts), the rushed process, and a desire to first discuss funding options with the City Council. The administration had presented this budget on March 23, 2026, designed to address a significant financial crisis with a 6% local tax increase. Earlier, on March 9, 2026, the administration presented an FY2027 budget proposal requiring approximately $8.4 million in reductions from the roll-forward budget to meet the City Council's 6% tax increase guidance, resulting in a 3.3% increase over the FY26 budget, the smallest in five years due to the depletion of the fund balance.

The district's budget challenges were evident from early discussions. On March 2, 2026, the board chair clarified that $7-8 million in cuts were necessary to present a budget with a 6% increase to the city council. On February 4, 2026, Dr. Johanna Prince presented a projected $7.2 million budget gap for FY2027, caused by declining student enrollment, rising staffing levels, increased costs, and a depleted fund balance. Maintaining current services would have required an 18.95% tax increase, but the board had set a target ceiling of 6%, necessitating significant cuts. The board began its FY2027 budget development process on December 17, 2025, reviewing financial forecasts and providing initial guidance, and announced a public budget forum on January 12, 2026, to gather input on creative cost-saving measures.

perspectives.Board: The board unanimously passed the final FY2027 budget, adopting the City Council's guidance for a 6% tax impact and approving a resolution to delay the reconfiguration timeline (April 29, 2026). Previously, the board failed to pass the Superintendent's initial FY2027 budget proposal due to concerns over specific personnel cuts (DEI, special education, arts), the rushed process, and a desire to discuss funding with the City Council (March 30, 2026). They had set a target ceiling of 6% for the tax increase (February 4, 2026) and discussed the challenging budget and significant shortfall (February 9, 2026). The board began the budget development process and provided initial guidance to the superintendent (December 17, 2025), also announcing a public forum to seek input (January 12, 2026).
perspectives.Administration: The Finance Director detailed the district's precarious financial state and the need for long-term stability, highlighting the City Council's offer to forgive up to $2 million of the current year's deficit (April 29, 2026). The Finance Director also presented the FY27 budget with a more realistic approach to expenses like electricity (April 2, 2026). The Superintendent's proposed FY2027 budget, designed to address a significant financial crisis, failed to pass (March 30, 2026), but was presented on March 23, 2026, aiming for fiscal sustainability with a 6% local tax increase. Earlier, the administration presented a proposal requiring $8.4 million in reductions to meet the 6% tax increase guidance (March 9, 2026), and highlighted the need for $7-8 million in cuts (March 2, 2026). Dr. Johanna Prince presented the major financial challenge for FY2027, detailing a projected $7.2 million budget gap due to various factors (February 4, 2026).
perspectives.Citizens: Public forums revealed a community desire for student-centered decisions and long-term fiscal stability (February 9, 2026). Public input on creative cost-saving measures was sought by the board (January 12, 2026).

Facilities.current_status: Remediation for the South Portland Middle School field is planned for Spring 2026 to ensure playability by Fall 2026, with the district not covering the costs. Major summer facilities projects, including security camera installations, secure vestibules, and roofing work, are either underway or completed at elementary schools.
Facilities.overview:
Recent developments include an update on the South Portland Middle School field on January 12, 2026, detailing a plan for aeration, overseeding, and fertilization in the spring to make it playable by Fall 2026, with the district maintaining it will not pay for the remediation. This follows a report on November 3, 2025, by the Director of Operations regarding significant soil and turf issues at the field and a multi-step remediation plan, where the board discussed holding the original contractor financially responsible. On July 14, 2025, major summer facilities projects were reported underway, including new surveillance camera systems and secure vestibules at all five elementary schools, alongside roofing work at Small, Kaler, and Skillin schools. The Director of Operations had announced on June 9, 2025, that security cameras would be installed in all five elementary schools over the summer, and new secure vestibules would be constructed at Brown, Kaler, and Small elementary schools that summer, with Skillin and Dyer scheduled for summer 2026. Earlier, on January 13, 2025, the Buildings and Grounds Committee reported on ongoing HVAC issues at the middle school, which were improving but still required significant staff time, and provided updates on the timeline for projects funded by recently passed school safety and maintenance bonds, with roof repairs and security camera installations potentially starting that summer.

Prior to these developments, on November 12, 2024, following the failure of the athletic complex referendum, the administration decided to pause and research before reintroducing the proposal to the board. A discussion also took place regarding moving the high school graduation from the stadium due to weather and field conditions, to a larger venue to accommodate more family members, with the board supporting surveying families and students for input. On June 10, 2024, the Administration presented a potential bond referendum of up to $17 million to address major facility needs, encompassing security enhancements at elementary schools, deferred maintenance like roofing and windows, and a complete renovation of the SPHS stadium complex. In response, the Board voted unanimously to direct the administration to prepare three separate bond referendum proposals—one for security, one for deferred maintenance, and one for athletic facilities—to allow for independent consideration and voting. This comprehensive approach was previewed by the Superintendent on May 13, 2024, who reported on declining student enrollment and an upcoming workshop on major facilities needs, including security upgrades, deferred maintenance, and the high school stadium overhaul.

Providing context for the stadium project's initial push, on July 8, 2024, numerous citizens, including parents and youth sports coaches, spoke in strong support of all three referenda, particularly the stadium project. They highlighted the poor condition of the current field, the critical need for reliable and safe facilities, and the perceived embarrassment of having substandard facilities compared to neighboring towns.

perspectives.Board: On November 3, 2025, the board discussed holding the original contractor financially responsible for the necessary repairs to the South Portland Middle School field. Following the failure of the athletic complex referendum, on November 12, 2024, the board supported surveying families and students for input regarding moving the high school graduation venue. On June 10, 2024, the Board voted unanimously to direct the administration to prepare three separate bond referendum proposals—one for security, one for deferred maintenance, and one for athletic facilities—after the administration had proposed a single, comprehensive bond.
perspectives.Administration: On January 12, 2026, the district maintained its stance that it would not pay for the remediation of the South Portland Middle School field. The Director of Operations reported on November 3, 2025, about significant soil and turf issues at the middle school field and outlined a multi-step remediation plan. On June 9, 2025, the Director of Operations announced the installation schedule for security cameras in all five elementary schools and the construction timeline for secure vestibules. On November 12, 2024, the administration decided to pause and research before reintroducing the athletic complex referendum after its failure. Earlier, on June 10, 2024, the Administration presented a potential bond referendum of up to $17 million to address major facility needs, including security, deferred maintenance, and stadium renovation. The Superintendent reported on May 13, 2024, that declining student enrollment would negatively impact state subsidy and previewed an upcoming workshop on major facilities needs.
perspectives.Staff: On January 13, 2025, the Buildings and Grounds Committee reported that ongoing HVAC issues at the middle school, while improving, still required significant staff time.
perspectives.Citizens: On July 8, 2024, numerous citizens, including parents and youth sports coaches, spoke in strong support of all three proposed referenda, especially the stadium project. They emphasized the poor condition of the current field, the necessity for reliable and safe facilities, and the embarrassment of having substandard facilities compared to neighboring towns.

Kaler Closure.current_status: The closure of Kaler Elementary School is progressing, with a parent survey distributed to gather input on student placement priorities for the upcoming school year. An elementary reconfiguration steering committee is also actively meeting.
Kaler Closure.overview:
On May 11, 2026, an update was provided regarding the ongoing elementary reconfiguration efforts. This update confirmed that a 23-member elementary reconfiguration steering committee is active and its meetings are open to the public. Crucially, concerning the Kaler Elementary School closure, a parent survey was distributed to solicit input on student placement priorities for the upcoming academic year.

This indicates that the process for closing Kaler Elementary School is moving forward, with administrative steps being taken to manage the transition of students. The involvement of a steering committee and the public nature of its meetings suggest a structured approach to the broader reconfiguration, of which the Kaler closure is a part.

perspectives.Citizens: On May 11, 2026, a parent survey was distributed to gather input on student placement priorities for the upcoming school year, directly soliciting feedback from the community regarding the Kaler Elementary School closure.

Reconfiguration.current_status: The SPSD Board is currently holding workshops on elementary school reconfiguration, focusing on addressing socioeconomic and demographic imbalances. The implementation of a new reconfiguration model has been delayed until the 2027-28 school year, with a steering committee established and a final vote on the plan expected by November 2026.
Reconfiguration.overview:
The SPSD Board is actively engaged in the reconfiguration process, with the first of several workshops on elementary school reconfiguration held on July 20, 2026. During this workshop, the board and public participated in an activity to rank priorities, with board members emphasizing the need to address socioeconomic and demographic imbalances between schools. This follows an update on May 11, 2026, regarding the 23-member elementary reconfiguration steering committee, whose meetings are open to the public, and a parent survey distributed for Kaler Elementary School closure student placement. On April 29, 2026, the board, in a 5-1 vote, approved a resolution to delay the reconfiguration timeline until the 2027-28 school year, establishing a steering committee and committing to a final vote on the implementation plan by November 2026. This decision effectively reversed the board's earlier vote on March 30, 2026, to implement a new model for the 2026-2027 school year.

Prior to this delay, on March 30, 2026, the Board had voted 4-2 to select 'Option A' to reconfigure the remaining elementary schools into a Primary (Pre-K to 1st grade) and Intermediate (2nd to 4th grade) model, effective for the 2026-2027 school year, citing long-term equity and efficiency benefits. This decision came after the administration presented nine detailed scenarios on March 2, 2026, to address a budget shortfall, primarily focused on reconfiguring the five elementary schools. The administration's rationale for reconfiguration included addressing declining enrollment, creating more equitable demographic balances across schools, and increasing opportunities for teacher collaboration. On February 9, 2026, the board had unanimously voted to request a formal proposal from the superintendent on the benefits and impacts of reconfiguring the district's elementary schools, stressing the need for data and community input.

Earlier efforts to address school configuration and equity issues date back to May 13, 2024, when the board approved a path forward based on recommendations from the Elementary Boundaries and Configuration Steering Committee. Key actions included reviewing the Brick Hill neighborhood's school assignment, providing more resources to schools with higher economic disadvantage, creating a policy for regular attendance zone review, and hiring a consultant to analyze attendance zones, configurations, and controlled choice/magnet models, with findings due by January 2025. On December 17, 2025, board members debated revisiting elementary school reconfiguration as a cost-saving measure, acknowledging complex equity issues of racial segregation between schools that had been identified by a previous committee.

perspectives.Board: Board members, on July 20, 2026, provided initial guidance emphasizing the need to address socioeconomic and demographic imbalances between schools. On April 29, 2026, they deliberated conflicting emotions, weighing requests for more planning time against the urgency to address equity and promises made to the Kaler community, ultimately voting 5-1 to delay reconfiguration until the 2027-28 school year and establish a steering committee. This reversed their March 30, 2026, 4-2 vote to implement 'Option A' (Primary/Intermediate model) for the 2026-2027 school year, which proponents cited for long-term equity and efficiency. On February 9, 2026, the board unanimously voted to request a formal proposal from the superintendent on reconfiguration, stressing data and community input. Earlier, on December 17, 2025, they debated revisiting reconfiguration as a cost-saving measure, acknowledging complex equity issues. On May 13, 2024, the board engaged in a lengthy debate, approving a path forward including hiring a consultant and reviewing attendance zones, grappling with the tension between maintaining neighborhood schools and creating integrated learning environments on April 8, 2024.
perspectives.Administration: The administration, on July 20, 2026, participated in a priority ranking activity for elementary school reconfiguration. On May 11, 2026, an update was provided on the 23-member elementary reconfiguration steering committee, and a parent survey was distributed for Kaler Elementary School student placement. On April 29, 2026, principals presented findings from extensive community listening sessions, and the administration requested more planning time for reconfiguration. On March 9, 2026, the administration presented a revised proposal to close Dyer Elementary School, keeping the remaining four schools in a Pre-K/K-4 configuration. On March 2, 2026, they presented nine detailed scenarios to address a budget shortfall, with the rationale for reconfiguration being to address declining enrollment, create more equitable demographic balances, and increase opportunities for teacher collaboration.
perspectives.Staff: Staff, particularly Kaler and Skillin staff, often prioritized equity in community listening sessions on April 29, 2026. Some teachers urged immediate reconfiguration, arguing delay perpetuates inequity, while others advocated for delay, citing the need for a more thorough, evidence-based process. On April 2, 2026, and March 30, 2026, teachers voiced strong opposition to the rushed reconfiguration timeline, citing a lack of a detailed plan, inadequate community input, and significant concerns about the impact on students, families, staff morale, and potential staff cuts to programs like music and special education. On March 2, 2026, public comment from teachers was overwhelmingly against reconfiguration, raising concerns about children's stability, loss of community schools, logistical challenges, the rushed timeline, and a lack of effective communication.
perspectives.Citizens: Citizens participated in a priority ranking activity during the first reconfiguration workshop on July 20, 2026. On May 11, 2026, a parent survey was distributed to gather input on student placement priorities for Kaler Elementary. On April 29, 2026, public comment revealed a deeply divided community, with some parents urging immediate reconfiguration to address inequity and honor promises to Kaler, while others advocated for delay, citing the need for a thorough process and concerns about neighborhood schools and young students. On April 2, 2026, and March 30, 2026, parents and students voiced strong opposition to the rushed timeline, lack of detailed plans, inadequate community input, and concerns about staff cuts and transparency. On March 2, 2026, public comment was overwhelmingly against reconfiguration, citing concerns about children's stability, loss of community schools, logistical challenges, and the rushed timeline. On February 4, 2026, citizens raised concerns about potential impacts like busing costs and class sizes. On May 13, 2024, several parents urged the board to ensure outside experts lead analysis, broaden community and teacher engagement, and not lose momentum in addressing demographic and socioeconomic segregation. On January 8, 2024, a community member urged the board to prepare for difficult conversations regarding school boundaries and reconfiguration.

Special Education.current_status: The district is currently navigating increased special education responsibilities due to new state mandates for pre-K services, while simultaneously facing budget cuts that eliminate two elementary occupational therapist positions, raising concerns about service delivery and legal compliance.
Special Education.overview:
On March 23, 2026, the district reported a special education population of 23% and discussed budget plans that include eliminating two elementary occupational therapist positions. These cuts raised concerns regarding student safety and the district's ability to meet legally mandated service requirements. This development follows the March 2, 2026 discussion where the district outlined plans for new state mandates, requiring it to assume responsibility for special education services for 4-year-olds in the next school year and 3-year-olds the year after, which will significantly increase the number of students served.

Prior to these discussions, on April 30, 2025, the Assistant Superintendent confirmed that the district was in a 'fact-finding' phase concerning the multi-year transition of pre-K special education services from Child Development Services (CDS) to the district, in response to a public question.

Further back, on March 25, 2024, the Director of Special Education presented a comprehensive overview of the department, which at that time served 649 students. The presentation detailed the types of disabilities addressed, the range of services provided, the Individualized Education Program (IEP) process, and emphasized the importance of delivering services in the least restrictive environment.

perspectives.Administration: The Assistant Superintendent indicated on April 30, 2025, that the district was in a 'fact-finding' phase regarding the pre-K special education transition. The Director of Special Education provided a detailed overview of the department's services on March 25, 2024. The administration is also planning for new state mandates to assume responsibility for pre-K special education services, as discussed on March 2, 2026.
perspectives.Citizens: Concerns were raised on March 23, 2026, regarding student safety and the district's ability to meet legally mandated service requirements due to the elimination of occupational therapist positions. A public question was also posed on April 30, 2025, regarding the pre-K special education transition.

Student Recognition.current_status: The SPSD Board continues to actively recognize student achievements across various domains, with the most recent celebration honoring the South Portland High School Top Scholars for 2026. This ongoing practice highlights academic excellence, athletic success, and artistic accomplishments.
Student Recognition.overview:
On May 11, 2026, the SPSD Board celebrated the South Portland High School Top Scholars for 2026, featuring students introducing their peers and sharing their academic achievements, extracurricular involvement, and future plans. This followed a November 3, 2025, recognition of the South Portland High School marching band for winning a gold medal and a five-star rating at the Maine Band Directors Association state finals.

Earlier, on May 27, 2025, the SPHS Robotics Team 58, the Riot Crew, was recognized for their impressive performance at the World Championships in Houston, where they ranked in the top 3%. The team demonstrated their robot for the board and received certificates of recognition. This recognition stemmed from an announcement on March 24, 2025, by the Superintendent that the team had qualified for the World Championships, with the district pledging financial support to ensure their participation.

Further back, on March 10, 2025, the board celebrated the South Portland High School Girls' Basketball team for winning the state championship. In the same meeting, three SPHS students were recognized for their Scholastic Art Awards, showcasing a commitment to acknowledging diverse student talents.

perspectives.Board: The Board consistently engages in direct recognition of student achievements, celebrating academic excellence (Top Scholars), athletic victories (Girls' Basketball, Marching Band), artistic talents (Scholastic Art Awards), and competitive success (Robotics Team).
perspectives.Administration: The Superintendent actively supports student participation in high-level competitions, as evidenced by the announcement on March 24, 2025, of the SPHS Robotics Team's qualification for the World Championships and the district's pledge of financial support.

Superintendent Search.current_status: The SPSD Board has identified a preferred candidate for the superintendent position and has authorized contract negotiations. A public announcement will be made once negotiations are complete.
Superintendent Search.overview:
On May 11, 2026, the board announced it had identified a preferred candidate for the superintendent position and unanimously voted to authorize the chair to enter into contract negotiations, with a public announcement pending the conclusion of these negotiations. Prior to this, on April 29, 2026, the Board announced two finalists and scheduled a community meet-and-greet for May 6th. The search process, confirmed by the Board Chair on March 9, 2026, was guided by Zeal Education Group and involved confidential interviews conducted solely by the school board and its student representatives.

The search for a new superintendent officially got underway with Zeal Education Group facilitating community feedback through on-site meetings and a Thought Exchange survey, as noted on February 9, 2026. On the same date, the board approved a one-time exception allowing student representatives to participate in semi-finalist interviews under strict confidentiality rules. Earlier, on February 4, 2026, a Board member made a direct appeal for greater community participation in feedback sessions due to low attendance. The board formally approved a contract with Zeal Education Group to conduct the superintendent search on January 12, 2026, also approving additional funds for national advertising and comprehensive background checks. Workshops and community forums were planned with Zeal Education Group, with a public workshop on December 22nd and a community forum on January 22nd, as announced on December 17, 2025. On December 8, 2025, a workshop was scheduled for December 10th where three firms—Maine School Management Association (MSMA), New England School Development Council (NESDEC), and Zeal Education Group—were to present their proposals.

The search for a new superintendent began following a board vote on June 18, 2025, to initiate a search for an interim superintendent. On the same date, the board voted to engage the Maine School Management Association (MSMA) to assist in the interim search and passed a motion to authorize the board chair and legal counsel to negotiate a separation agreement with Superintendent Metheny, contingent upon a successful interim superintendent search. Board members also discussed the importance of leadership stability, expressing openness to having an interim superintendent serve for the entire school year to minimize transitions.

perspectives.Board: The Board has consistently driven the search process, from initiating the interim search and negotiating Superintendent Metheny's separation on June 18, 2025, to selecting Zeal Education Group for the full search on January 12, 2026. They approved student representatives in semi-finalist interviews on February 9, 2026, and announced two finalists on April 29, 2026. Most recently, on May 11, 2026, they unanimously authorized contract negotiations with a preferred candidate. A Board member also expressed concern about low community feedback participation on February 4, 2026, and on June 18, 2025, members discussed the importance of leadership stability.
perspectives.Administration: On April 29, 2026, several administrators voiced strong disappointment with the closed superintendent search process, arguing that the lack of stakeholder involvement and transparency was contrary to the board's stated values.
perspectives.Staff: On April 29, 2026, union leaders from SPTA and SPESPA voiced strong disappointment with the closed superintendent search process, stating that the lack of stakeholder involvement and transparency devalued the expertise of district employees.

Transportation.current_status: The district has committed to providing three buses for large track meets and engaged a consultant to re-optimize all bus routes for the upcoming school year to address overcrowding, particularly in the Brick Hill area.
Transportation.overview:
On June 8, 2026, the administration presented detailed plans to address recent transportation complaints. These plans included a commitment to providing three buses for large track meets and engaging a consultant to re-optimize all bus routes for the next school year. The goal of this re-optimization is to alleviate overcrowding, particularly in the Brick Hill area.

These administrative actions followed significant safety concerns raised on May 11, 2026. During public comment, parents and a transportation employee highlighted severe overcrowding on buses for athletic events and regular morning routes, with students reportedly sitting in aisles. In response to these concerns, the superintendent pledged to investigate the issue immediately.

perspectives.Administration: On May 11, 2026, the superintendent pledged to investigate significant bus overcrowding issues immediately. By June 8, 2026, the administration presented detailed plans, committing to providing three buses for large track meets and engaging a consultant to re-optimize all bus routes for the next school year to alleviate overcrowding, especially in the Brick Hill area.
perspectives.Staff: On May 11, 2026, a transportation employee raised significant safety concerns regarding severe overcrowding on buses for athletic events and regular morning routes, noting students sitting in aisles.
perspectives.Citizens: On May 11, 2026, parents raised significant safety concerns about severe overcrowding on buses for athletic events and regular morning routes, with reports of students sitting in aisles.

Adult Education.current_status: The Adult Education program is experiencing rapid growth, particularly in ESOL and new Integrated Education and Training (IET) programs. However, it faces a significant funding challenge due to its nearly 70% reliance on unstable grants, necessitating increased local investment for sustainability.
Adult Education.overview:
On December 9, 2024, the Director of Adult Education presented on the program's rapid growth, specifically mentioning ESOL services and the new Integrated Education and Training (IET) program. She highlighted a significant funding challenge, noting the program is nearly 70% reliant on unstable grants, and signaled a clear need for increased local investment in the upcoming budget to ensure the program's long-term sustainability.

This follows earlier reports of exponential growth. On March 25, 2024, the Director of Adult Education highlighted that the program had become the third largest in Maine. At that time, it was already noted as heavily reliant on grants, having expanded its ESOL classes to five levels and developing digital skills and job training programs to meet high community demand.

perspectives.Administration: The Administration, through the Director of Adult Education, has consistently reported rapid and exponential growth in the Adult Education program, particularly in ESOL and new IET/job training initiatives. They have identified a critical funding challenge, noting the program's nearly 70% reliance on unstable grants, and advocate for increased local investment to ensure its long-term sustainability.

Community School Model.current_status: The South Portland Middle School's Community School model has demonstrated positive outcomes and is being presented as a successful example, with a call for sustainable funding and potential district-wide expansion.
Community School Model.overview:
On October 15, 2024, the principal and community school director from South Portland Middle School delivered a detailed presentation to the board regarding their successful Community School model. They highlighted its six key practices and reported positive outcomes, including reduced chronic absenteeism and increased family engagement. The presentation emphasized the critical need for sustainable funding to ensure the model's continuation and to explore its potential expansion across the district.

This presentation marks the most recent development concerning the Community School Model, showcasing its current effectiveness at SPMS and initiating discussions around its broader implementation and financial support.

Snow Day Policy.current_status: The SPSD has implemented a new snow day policy, eliminating remote learning for the first five snow days and instead adding them to the end of the school year. This change was made due to concerns about remote learning's effectiveness for younger students.
Snow Day Policy.overview:
On November 12, 2024, the Administration announced a significant change to the snow day policy. This new policy eliminates remote learning days for the first five snow days, opting instead to add these days to the end of the school year. The Superintendent cited that remote learning days are not a good fit for the youngest learners as the primary reason for this modification.

The South Portland Teacher Association (SPTA) representatives voiced concerns regarding this policy shift during the November 12, 2024 meeting. They highlighted that staff had made plans based on the previously approved calendar and the established practice of utilizing remote days for inclement weather. The SPTA urged the board to engage in collaborative discussions with educators to develop a more equitable and effective plan for managing snow days.

perspectives.Administration: On November 12, 2024, the Superintendent announced the elimination of remote learning for the first five snow days, stating these days would instead be added to the end of the school year. This decision was based on the belief that remote learning is not effective for the youngest learners.
perspectives.Staff: During the November 12, 2024 meeting, the South Portland Teacher Association (SPTA) representatives expressed concern about the new snow day policy. They noted that staff had already made plans according to the prior calendar and the practice of remote learning days, advocating for collaboration with educators to create a more equitable and effective inclement weather plan.

Student Achievement.current_status: Approximately half of students meet grade-level benchmarks according to NWEA MAP data, while SAT scores remain below state and national averages. The administration recognizes the need to focus on improving these outcomes to support students' post-secondary goals.
Student Achievement.overview:
On January 22, 2024, the Superintendent presented key data points regarding student achievement. This included NWEA MAP results, which indicated that roughly half of students are meeting grade-level benchmarks and about 40% are achieving their growth targets. Furthermore, the report highlighted that SAT scores continue to be below both state and national averages, a concern the administration acknowledged as a critical area requiring focused attention to ensure students are adequately prepared for their post-secondary aspirations.

There are no prior decisions or developments mentioned in the provided notes that have been reversed or modified by this recent update.

perspectives.Administration: The Superintendent shared NWEA MAP data indicating that roughly half of students meet grade-level benchmarks and about 40% meet growth targets. The administration acknowledged that SAT scores remaining below state and national averages is an area needing focus to ensure students can achieve their post-secondary goals.

Student Mental Health.current_status: The district is actively focusing on student mental health through family nights, virtual forums, and partnerships with organizations like NAMI and AFSP, following recent tragedies. New initiatives include universal screeners, a formal mental health action plan, and the recent hiring of a Director of Mental and Behavioral Health.
Student Mental Health.overview:
On October 15, 2024, the student representative reported on school activities, including a family night focused on mental health. The high school principal and superintendent further elaborated on this event and a separate virtual forum, highlighting the district's ongoing commitment to student mental health and its partnerships with organizations such as NAMI and the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention.

Prior to this, on September 9, 2024, the Administration addressed the tragic suicides of three students, acknowledging the severity of the situation. The Superintendent detailed the existing mental health resources available and outlined significant future actions, which included the implementation of universal screeners, the development of a formal mental health action plan, and the welcoming of the district's first Director of Mental and Behavioral Health.

perspectives.Administration: On October 15, 2024, the high school principal and superintendent elaborated on district efforts, including family nights and virtual forums, and highlighted partnerships with NAMI and the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention. On September 9, 2024, the Superintendent addressed recent student suicides, detailed current resources, and outlined future actions such as universal screeners, a formal mental health action plan, and the hiring of a Director of Mental and Behavioral Health.

AI in Education.current_status: The SPSD has adopted "Magic School AI" as a controlled tool and is developing comprehensive training and curriculum for its integration into education.
AI in Education.overview: On July 8, 2024, the Technology Director presented the AI Steering Committee's recent work to the board. Key developments included the adoption of "Magic School AI" as a controlled tool for the district, the ongoing development of staff competency training programs, and the creation of a dedicated curriculum for students focusing on AI. During this meeting, the board engaged in discussions concerning the critical balance between leveraging the benefits of AI in education and ensuring the preservation of essential skills, such as writing, among students.

perspectives.Board: The board discussed the challenge of balancing the benefits offered by AI with the necessity of preserving essential student skills, particularly writing.
perspectives.Administration: The Technology Director presented the AI Steering Committee's work, which included the adoption of "Magic School AI" as a controlled tool, the development of staff competency training, and the creation of a student curriculum.

District Goals.current_status: The district's 2024-2025 'Pillars and Priorities' have been presented, focusing on improving student engagement, reducing chronic absenteeism, and expanding mental and behavioral health supports. These priorities align with the recently introduced 'Together We Grow' theme and four key pillars.
District Goals.overview:
On September 9, 2024, the Administration presented the district's four 'Pillars and Priorities' for the 2024-2025 school year. Key goals outlined include improving student engagement, reducing chronic absenteeism by another 5%, and continuing to build out mental and behavioral health supports.

This presentation followed the Superintendent's introduction on August 19, 2024, of the 2024-25 district theme, "Together We Grow." During this meeting, four key pillars were outlined: Instructional Excellence, DEIB, Operational Effectiveness, and a new pillar for Strategic Planning, which will address future school configurations and boundaries.

perspectives.Administration: On August 19, 2024, the Superintendent introduced the 2024-25 district theme, "Together We Grow," and outlined four key pillars for the year. Subsequently, on September 9, 2024, the Administration presented the specific 'Pillars and Priorities' for the 2024-2025 school year, detailing goals such as improving student engagement, reducing chronic absenteeism by 5%, and enhancing mental and behavioral health supports.

K-4 Math Curriculum.current_status: The SPSD Board is currently considering the adoption of the 'Into Math' program for K-4, which would replace the long-standing 'Investigations' curriculum. A vote on this quarter-million-dollar adoption is scheduled for January.
K-4 Math Curriculum.overview: On December 9, 2024, the Director of Curriculum formally recommended the adoption of the 'Into Math' program for grades K-4. This new curriculum is proposed to replace the 'Investigations' curriculum, which has been in use for 20 years. The recommendation emerged from a thorough review process conducted by a committee of educators. During the meeting, the Board engaged in discussions regarding the implications of this transition for both teachers and families, with a particular focus on multilingual learners. The Board is slated to vote on this significant quarter-million-dollar adoption in January.

perspectives.Board: The Board discussed the practical aspects of transitioning to a new curriculum, specifically considering the impact on teachers and multilingual learners. They are scheduled to vote on the proposed adoption in January.
perspectives.Administration: The Director of Curriculum recommended the adoption of the 'Into Math' program for K-4, based on a thorough review process conducted by an educator committee, to replace the existing 20-year-old 'Investigations' curriculum.
perspectives.Staff: Educators participated in a committee that conducted a thorough review process, leading to the recommendation of the 'Into Math' program for K-4.

Mental & Behavioral Health.current_status: The new Director of Mental and Behavioral Health is prioritizing suicide prevention, intervention, and postvention, and is actively seeking grant funding to enhance mental health services.
Mental & Behavioral Health.overview: On December 9, 2024, the new Director of Mental and Behavioral Health provided an update to the board. Her presentation highlighted the department's renewed focus on suicide prevention, intervention, and postvention, a response prompted by recent community tragedies. She also detailed ongoing partnerships with national and local organizations and announced a grant application with SoPo Unite for opioid settlement funds, aimed at enhancing mental health services within the district.

perspectives.Administration: On December 9, 2024, the new Director of Mental and Behavioral Health updated the board on the department's focus on suicide prevention, intervention, and postvention, citing recent community tragedies. She also reported on partnerships with national and local organizations and a grant application with SoPo Unite for opioid settlement funds to enhance mental health services.

School Climate.current_status: Panorama survey data indicates that while younger students feel safe, older students (grades 6-12) report a low sense of belonging, reinforcing the district's "You Belong Here" initiative.
School Climate.overview: On January 22, 2024, the district reviewed Panorama survey data concerning school climate. The findings highlighted that younger students generally feel safe within the school environment. However, a significant concern emerged regarding older students (grades 6-12), with only 41% reporting a favorable sense of belonging. This data is being used to reinforce the district's ongoing "You Belong Here" theme, aiming to improve the overall school climate, particularly for secondary students.

Service Employees Contract.current_status: The SPSD Board ratified a three-year contract (FY25-27) with the South Portland School District Service Employees Association (SPESPA) on November 12, 2024.
Service Employees Contract.overview: On November 12, 2024, the SPSD Board ratified a three-year contract covering fiscal years 2025-2027 with the South Portland School District Service Employees Association (SPESPA). Both the board's negotiating team and the superintendent commended the collaborative and professional approach taken during the negotiation process.

perspectives.Board: On November 12, 2024, the board ratified the three-year contract with SPESPA, with their negotiating team praising the collaborative and professional nature of the negotiations.
perspectives.Administration: On November 12, 2024, the superintendent praised the collaborative and professional nature of the negotiations that led to the ratification of the SPESPA contract.

Student Data.current_status: Recent data from SPHS indicates positive trends in student outcomes, with significant reductions in chronic absenteeism, out-of-school suspensions, and course failure rates. These improvements suggest effective strategies are in place.
Student Data.overview: On July 8, 2024, the new SPHS Principal presented encouraging student data trends to the board. The report highlighted a notable decrease in chronic absenteeism, which dropped from 42.3% to 35.5%. Furthermore, out-of-school suspensions saw a substantial 66% reduction, and the course failure rate improved from 6.7% to 4.4%.

perspectives.Administration: The SPHS Principal presented positive data trends, indicating improvements in chronic absenteeism, out-of-school suspensions, and course failure rates at the high school.

Student Support Systems.current_status: Principals recently provided a detailed presentation on the Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) framework, outlining its application for academic and behavioral interventions across all school levels.
Student Support Systems.overview: On March 18, 2024, principals from the elementary, middle, and high schools delivered comprehensive presentations to the board. Their focus was on the Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) framework, explaining its implementation to identify and support struggling students. The presentations detailed how MTSS utilizes universal, targeted, and intensive interventions to ensure student success in both academic and behavioral domains.

Student Enrollment.current_status: Declining student enrollment is a significant factor contributing to a projected $7.2 million budget gap for FY2027, necessitating substantial cuts to maintain the district's financial stability.
Student Enrollment.overview: On February 4, 2026, the Administration, led by Dr. Johanna Prince, presented a critical financial challenge for the upcoming FY2027 budget. A major contributing factor to a projected $7.2 million budget gap is declining student enrollment, alongside rising staffing levels, increased costs, and a depleted fund balance. This situation necessitates significant cuts to district services, as maintaining current services would require an 18.95% tax increase, far exceeding the board's target ceiling of 6%.

perspectives.Administration: The Administration, through Dr. Johanna Prince, identified declining student enrollment as a key driver of the projected $7.2 million budget deficit for FY2027, highlighting its impact on the district's financial health.

Board Governance.current_status: Serious concerns about board governance, including lack of public notice and an un-agendized compensation vote, were raised on June 8, 2026. Several board members publicly apologized for the rushed decision and breakdown in transparency.
Board Governance.overview: On June 8, 2026, significant issues concerning board governance came to the forefront, drawing criticism from both public commenters and board members themselves. The core of these concerns revolved around the lack of adequate public notice for a special meeting and the controversial inclusion of an un-agendized vote on compensation. In response, board members Feller, Richardson, and Holman publicly expressed regret, acknowledging that the decision was rushed, that they had misjudged public sentiment during a period of financial austerity, and that there had been a clear failure in maintaining transparency. These events highlighted a perceived breakdown in established governance protocols and public trust.

perspectives.Board: On June 8, 2026, several board members, including Feller, Richardson, and Holman, publicly apologized for a rushed decision, failing to "read the room" during austerity, and a breakdown in transparency related to board governance. They also raised concerns about the lack of public notice for a special meeting and an un-agendized compensation vote.
perspectives.Citizens: Public commenters on June 8, 2026, raised serious concerns about board governance, specifically citing the lack of public notice for a special meeting and the addition of an un-agendized compensation vote.

Student Cell Phone Policy 2026.current_status: The SPSD Board recently approved the second read of a new state-mandated cell phone policy (JICI) requiring phones to be off and away bell-to-bell. Specific implementation procedures will be developed at the school level and reviewed by the board later.
Student Cell Phone Policy 2026.overview:
On July 20, 2026, the board approved the second read of a new state-mandated cell phone policy, designated as JICI. This policy mandates that student cell phones must be off and away for the duration of the school day, from bell to bell.

During the discussion on July 20, 2026, it was clarified that while the core policy itself is now established, the detailed procedures for its implementation will be developed at the individual school level. These school-specific implementation plans will subsequently be brought before the board for review at a later date.

perspectives.Board: On July 20, 2026, the board approved the second read of the state-mandated cell phone policy (JICI) and engaged in a lengthy discussion to clarify that implementation procedures would be developed at the school level and reviewed later.
perspectives.Administration: On July 20, 2026, the administration was involved in the discussion clarifying that school-level implementation procedures would be developed and later reviewed by the board, following the approval of the state-mandated policy.

Administrators Contract 2025-2028.current_status: The 2025-2028 Administrators Contract has been unanimously ratified by the board, marking the first of three major contracts to be settled.
Administrators Contract 2025-2028.overview: On August 18, 2025, the board unanimously ratified a three-year collective bargaining agreement (2025-2028) with the South Portland Administrators Association. This agreement is significant as it is the first of three major contracts to be settled.

perspectives.Board: The board unanimously ratified the three-year collective bargaining agreement with the South Portland Administrators Association.
